newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL - "STATEMENT GAME" OR NOT, RODMAN LAUGHS OFF LOSS TO KNICKS.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL - "STATEMENT GAME" OR NOT, RODMAN LAUGHS OFF LOSS TO KNICKS.

text.p: While others debated whether the Knicks' win over the Chicago Bulls was a "statement game," an unconcerned Dennis Rodman was frolicking in the New York cheerleaders' room with his pro wrestler buddy Hulk Hogan.

"We didn't play well and we almost beat them," said the Bulls' rebounding specialist, his hairstyle du jour like a cyclist's multi-coloured racing helmet -- a front-to-back red stripe on top of a mostly blond upside-down bowl.

After Sunday's 97-93 loss, Rodman said he still did not think the Bulls, who have by far the best record in the NBA, would necessarily face New York, narrowly second best in the league, in the Eastern Conference finals.

"I don't think the Knicks are the team we have to beat in the playoffs. They have to get there first. Who will they play in the first round, Miami, Charlotte, Washington, who knows? They need to get through two rounds to get to us."

Rodman -- who took off his earrings to show Hogan what they were doing to his earlobes, then let the brawny showman help him put them back on -- added confidently: "If we do play the Knicks I know we'll go to the finals."

Hogan, a Chicagoan, seemed more upset about the loss than Rodman. But both were having a rollicking good time flirting with Knick dancer/cheerleaders until they were chased out of the room, which is across the hall from the visiting team's locker room at Madison Square Garden.
"Dennis Rodman did his job," said Hogan. "He played a great game. The Bulls didn't back him up by shooting the ball very well. Rodman is the best, second only to Michael."
Michael Jordan scored a game-high 36 points but went just 14-for-31 from the field. Rodman had 19 rebounds and nine points.

Rodman looked like he was practicing some of Hogan's wrestling moves during the game, at one point throwing New York centre Patrick Ewing to the floor. "I just chopped Patrick, it's just in the game," he said.
"I thought what he did was unnecessary," said Ewing, who led the Knicks with 32 points and 14 rebounds. "He picked up my leg and body-slammed me. I didn't appreciate it. I could have gotten hurt."
"Dennis is crazy like a fox," said Chicago's Australian centre Luc Longley, who fouled out guarding Ewing. "He tried to get Patrick out of focus or maybe thrown out in a fight with him."

Of the game itself, Ewing said: "It's a big win against a great team. Chicago's the defending world champion and we showed that we're capable of beating them." But he added: "They already know we're for real."

Ewing scored the clinching basket with a 16-foot side jumper off glass with 7.7 seconds to go, then did a twirling dance past the Chicago bench. "It was a big shot. I did some celebrating," he admitted.
Ewing claimed he was fouled as he took the shot. "That made it hit off the glass and it still went in," he said with a big smile.

Chicago coach Phil Jackson saw it differently. "The shot wasn't going in, it banked off the backboard. It was a lucky shot. But Patrick even had a little ability to celebrate after that. I congratulate him for that. It takes a lot of nerve to celebrate one that you bank in from the side."
Jackson picked his words carefully in assessing the Knicks' playoff chances. "They certainly have the talent to be there. The bench strength is noticeable. Their bench outplayed our bench tonight."
Jackson pointed out that the Bulls had been without their first man off the bench, injured Croatian swingman Toni Kukoc.

The Chicago coach granted that the Knicks, the Atlantic Division leaders, "made a statement today by being able to beat us on their court." But the Central Division-leading Bulls are likely to hold homecourt advantage throughout the playoffs.
"We're playing for first in our conference. We want homecourt advantage," said Jackson.
"When it comes down to crunch time we're real confident about playing this team in this building. If they make the match, we're looking forward to that."
Jordan was a bit more generous to the Knicks than was his coach or Rodman.
"I don't think we played our best basketball but I don't feel we should take anything away from them. They came in with a little more intensity, a little more to prove," Jordan said.
He agreed the road to the championships goes through Chicago -- "It does!" he exclaimed -- but did not believe the Bulls' road necessarily went through New York.

"I'm not saying we can't get knocked down. I'm not saying someone can't take what we have. We just don't want to let it go. Everyone in the league knows that to get the championship in 1997 you have to go through Chicago."
While agreeing the revamped Knicks "on paper" have more scoring power than in previous seasons, Jordan said: "The dangerous aspect is from their leadership, the hunger that those players have."
Jordan, who has led the Bulls to four NBA championships said: "We've got to match that hunger."
